name: Furosemide
route_note: oral tablet or solution; IV or IM injection; subcutaneous on-body infusor (Furoscix)

discovery.note: A sulfamoylanthranilic acid derivative; introduced clinically in the early 1960s.

tagline: Potent loop diuretic for fluid overload, used since the 1960s
summary: Furosemide is a potent loop diuretic that blocks sodium, potassium and chloride reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. It is the standard treatment for fluid overload in heart failure, cirrhosis and kidney disease, and for acute pulmonary oedema.
mechanism: Furosemide is secreted into the tubule and inhibits the Na–K–2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2, SLC12A1) on the luminal membrane of the thick ascending limb, where about a quarter of filtered sodium is reabsorbed.

This causes a large natriuresis and diuresis and also increases excretion of potassium, calcium and magnesium. IV furosemide additionally causes venodilation, which relieves pulmonary congestion before diuresis begins.
uses: Oedema due to heart failure, cirrhosis or renal disease

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: Approved in the US as Lasix.

history.title: DOSE trial
history.detail: In acute heart failure, bolus versus continuous infusion and low versus high dose show no major difference in symptoms.

history.title: Subcutaneous form
history.detail: The FDA approves Furoscix, a subcutaneous on-body infusor for congestion in chronic heart failure.

history.title: TRANSFORM-HF
history.detail: Torsemide does not reduce mortality compared with furosemide after heart failure hospitalisation.

serious: Ototoxicity (high doses, rapid IV, with aminoglycosides)
safety.boxed_warning: Potent diuretic that, in excessive amounts, can lead to profound diuresis with water and electrolyte depletion; dose must be individualised under supervision.

facts: The brand name Lasix is said to come from 'lasts six hours'.
It is prohibited in sport by WADA as a diuretic and masking agent, and is widely used in racehorses.
